blocks.en:
Matter-of-Fact ( Jansen et al., 2025 ) , the closest work to our
task, evaluates separate baselines for literature retrieval and for code
generation. Unlike its binary labels, a five-point scale like SFBench’s
has a middle label, 0, with which an expert can record that a claim is too
underspecified to judge, as the expert who labeled our opening claim
did. In our experience,
Matter-of-Fact’s labels were also too noisy for comparing an agent’s
verdicts with gold labels claim by claim. We therefore took our
materials-science claims from SFBench, whose labels use a five-point scale
and come with an expert’s written rationale, and the rationales also let a judge model
compare a card with the expert’s interpretation
(Appendix G ).

accompanies a claim, and observe that justifications given for the claim
alone often rest on generic plausibility rather than on explicit
experimental constraints. Their models are given the context. Because our
agent gathers its own evidence and we vary the interpretation, their probes
do not carry over to our setting. Liu et al. (2026) build claims in which a less prominent
constraint is contradicted and find that verifiers often accept them.
Those claims contradict a stated constraint rather than omit one, so they
test whether a verifier checks every constraint a claim states, and we do
not use them. Listing each constraint as a card field might show which
ones a verifier tested. QuanTemp ( Venktesh et al., 2024 ) collects real-world numerical claims, many of which lack precise
information. Drawn from news and politics and labeled for veracity rather
than feasibility, its claims do not fit our task.

blocks.en:
We follow Pezzelle (2023) in treating underspecification as a normal
property of language, which readers resolve from context and shared
knowledge. In machine learning, D’Amour et al. (2022) call a training pipeline underspecified when it can return many models
with equally good held-out performance but different behavior in
deployment, and we use the term only for a claim that omits a detail
needed to assess it. Vijayvargiya et al. (2026) separate ambiguity from
underspecificity, and Kennedy (2011) separates ambiguity
from vagueness. By Kennedy’s distinction, an unstated threshold for
“significant” makes a claim vague rather than ambiguous. We use
ambiguity for the open choice among interpretations that
underspecification leaves, whatever its source. On DUST ( Wildenburg et al., 2024 ) , newer language models
identified underspecified sentences only moderately well when asked, and
interpreted them poorly and with little uncertainty, and crowdworkers judged GPT-4’s
disambiguations of AmbiEnt sentences correct far less often than the
dataset’s own ( Liu et al., 2023a ) . Models also fill in
requirements that a prompt leaves unstated, but underspecified prompts are
more likely to regress when the model or the prompt changes ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and adding explicit context to
underspecified queries can change evaluation conclusions ( Malaviya et al., 2025 ) . AmbigQA ( Min et al., 2020 ) tests whether models recover the
interpretations of ambiguous questions, CLAMBER ( Zhang et al., 2024b ) whether they identify ambiguous queries
and ask clarifying questions, and AmbiBench ( Tamkin et al., 2023 ) whether they infer the intended task from ambiguous instructions and
examples. We do not use these datasets, or AmbiEnt and DUST, because their
items are general-domain sentences, questions or instructions whose
interpretations were enumerated or categorized in advance, by annotators or
by construction. The ambiguity we study comes from domain details
that a scientific claim omits, and no dataset we know of lists the
interpretations of such a claim. Measures built on a list of interpretations, for example
whether a model recognizes the ambiguity or recovers each interpretation,
therefore do not apply. A card instead records the interpretation the
agent adopts, which shapes the evidence it seeks, and our measures relate
that interpretation to a verdict an expert has labeled. Disagreement among annotators of
inference items persists with more ratings and context ( Pavlick and Kwiatkowski, 2019 ) and partly traces to
underspecified meaning ( Jiang and de Marneffe, 2022 ) . By
analogy, the run-to-run variation in interpretation that we report may
reflect the claims themselves and not only sampling noise.

blocks.en:
In AmbiFC ( Glockner et al., 2024 ) , annotators’ disagreement about the
veracity of its roughly 10K claims
reflects ambiguity, which the authors trace partly to underspecification, and they train veracity
models on soft labels. Its claims are general-domain claims annotated
against evidence passages supplied with them, and its labels record how
annotators split rather than which interpretation a system adopted. Our
study needs claims that an expert labeled for feasibility and on which the
agent finds its own evidence, and AmbiFC’s claims offer neither. Whether the
fields a card marks as default predict where AmbiFC’s annotators disagree
is an open question. Dis2Dis ( Staliūnaitė and
Vlachos, 2025 ) rewrites an ambiguous claim so
that the given evidence supports one interpretation unequivocally. A Dis2Dis rewrite could serve as the claim that ClaimSpy assesses, though
we have not tested this. LIAR-New ( Pelrine et al., 2023 ) labels whether
a political statement has enough context to be judged, and Orlovskiy et al. (2024) ask the user for the information
an ambiguous statement leaves out. Benchmark claims have no author to
ask, so a card records the interpretation instead, and the fields it
marks as inferred or default show what such a question would ask about.
Claimify ( Metropolitansky and
Larson, 2025 ) extracts a claim only when it
is confident of the intended interpretation and otherwise flags the
sentence as one it cannot disambiguate, and decontextualization ( Choi et al., 2021 ) recovers missing details from a
source document. Neither applies here, because a feasibility assessment
must return a verdict on the claim as given and our claims come without a
source document. News reports and LLM summaries of scientific findings
often state them more generally than the original papers do ( Wuehrl et al., 2024 ; Peters and Chin-Yee, 2025 ) ,
a broadening that a card’s quantifier field could record. Joseph et al. (2026) , drawing on how clinical experts check
health claims, identify underspecified claims and mismatched intentions as
obstacles to end-to-end fact-checking, and they argue that fact-checking
should communicate with the user rather than end in a verdict.

blocks.en:
On underspecified
software tasks ( Vijayvargiya et al., 2026 ) , tool calls ( Wang et al., 2025 ) and user requests ( Qian et al., 2024 ) , agents usually fill the gaps with assumptions
rather than ask for the missing details. We do not use these benchmarks,
because none of their tasks is a claim to assess. Several methods decide
when and what to ask ( Rao and Daumé III, 2018 ; Zhang and Choi, 2025 ) . Other
methods answer under each interpretation and then combine or list the
answers ( Hou et al., 2024 ; Saparina and Lapata, 2026 ) , or use agreement among sampled answers to
decide when to abstain on an ambiguous question ( Cole et al., 2023 ) . Wen et al. (2025) survey
abstention, which in our setting means scoring 0. A card run without
computational libraries took 3.8 minutes and cost $0.27 on average, counted in GPT-5.4
tokens only and at list price (Appendix G ), and
running the agent once per interpretation would multiply that by the
number of interpretations, which grows quickly across nine fields.
Running an edited card next to the card it was edited from is a targeted
version of such an ensemble. Our five runs per claim resemble that
sampling, but we use them to measure how the interpretation varies, not to
decide when to abstain. Self-consistency ( Wang et al., 2023 ) samples several reasoning paths and keeps the most common answer, and a
vote over a claim’s runs would likewise hide which interpretation each
run used. Our consistency judge, which groups values that
express the same interpretation, resembles clustering sampled outputs by
meaning ( Kuhn et al., 2023 ) .
Analysts given the same data and hypothesis reach divergent conclusions
through different analytic choices, whether they are people ( Silberzahn et al., 2018 ; Schweinsberg et al., 2021 ) or LLM
agents ( Bertran et al., 2026 ) , and a multiverse analysis reports a
result across the defensible choices instead of one ( Steegen et al., 2016 ) . Reporting a verdict with the
interpretation it rests on applies the same idea to one choice at a
time. BLADE ( Gu et al., 2024 ) grades an
agent’s analytic choices against expert analyses, and DiscoveryBench ( Majumder et al., 2025 ) builds each goal so that it
leads to one answer, removing the ambiguity by construction. These
benchmarks pose questions about datasets, and our claims come without
data. They also assess an agent’s choices after the analysis, and a card
records the interpretation at the start of a run.

blocks.en:
LLM agents now plan and run
chemistry experiments ( Bran et al., 2024 ; Boiko et al., 2023 ) , synthesize literature ( Skarlinski et al., 2024 ) , retrieve materials data and run
atomistic simulations ( Chiang et al., 2025 ) , answer
materials-science questions from a curated knowledge base and general
tools ( Zhang et al., 2024a ) , and test hypotheses by sequential
falsification ( Huang et al., 2025 ) . In our runs with the
computational tools, the agent can call comparable tools, in which a coding agent
computes phase equilibria or runs a machine-learned interatomic potential
(Section 3 ). There we ask how the interpretation
adopted at the start of a run affects whether the agent calculates and what it
calculates (Section 4.6 ). Across many runs of science
agents in several domains, the base model explained far more of the
variation than the agent scaffold, and failures in how agents used
evidence were invisible to evaluation of outcomes alone ( Ríos-García et al., 2026 ) . Tool-calling agents are inconsistent
across repeated trials ( Yao et al., 2025 ) , and agent evaluations
seldom account for cost ( Kapoor et al., 2025 ) . Comparing ClaimSpy
with these agents would confound agent design with interpretation, since
this study keeps one agent and varies how its interpretation is recorded
or set. A card could be added to any of them.

blocks.en:
A model’s reasoning need not
reflect what drives its answer ( Turpin et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) , and an explanation can be plausible without
being faithful ( Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020 ) . A card is extracted
from the agent’s first reasoning step by another model, so the same
caution applies to it. In card mode the card reaches a run only through
the scorer and the report step, whereas in frozen mode it is a structured
instruction in the agent’s prompt. Changing a field can change the score,
and the edited value often reached the questions the agent sent to its
tools, the context it passed to the search agent and its final answer
(Section 4.3 ). Such an edit is like editing a concept of a
concept bottleneck model at test time ( Koh et al., 2020 ) . Interfaces that show a model’s interpretation
of a request, before it acts or as an explanation of its output, and let
users edit it have helped users steer or correct systems for text-to-SQL ( Tian et al., 2023 ) , end-user programming ( Liu et al., 2023b ) , data analysis ( Kazemitabaar et al., 2024 ) , code generation ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) and agent planning ( Feng et al., 2026 ) . A Claim Card is shown before
the agent’s first tool call runs (Section 2.2 ).
Explanations in automated fact-checking justify a verdict after the
evidence is gathered ( Atanasova et al., 2020 ) , while the
fact-checkers interviewed by Warren et al. (2025) asked for
explanations that show uncertainty and information gaps. Explanations can
also raise reliance on a system whether or not it is right ( Bansal et al., 2021 ) , a risk we return to in the Ethics
Statement.

blocks.en:
Structured representations record what a claim states. PICO frames
clinical evidence by population, intervention, comparator and outcome, the
elements that EBM-NLP ( Nye et al., 2018 ) annotates in trial
abstracts, and SciClaim ( Magnusson and Friedman, 2021 ) annotates the factors,
associations, magnitudes and qualifiers of scientific claims. Neither
records the threshold a claim must meet or where each value came from,
and neither carries feasibility labels, so their annotations could not
serve as cards or as gold labels here. FActScore ( Min et al., 2023 ) decomposes generated text into atomic
facts and scores each, whereas a card decomposes a claim
into the fields a feasibility assessment needs, including those the claim
leaves out. Model cards ( Mitchell et al., 2019 ) , datasheets ( Gebru et al., 2021 ) and data statements ( Bender and Friedman, 2018 ) record the assumptions behind a model or
a dataset for others to inspect, and preregistration ( Nosek et al., 2018 ) commits to hypotheses and analysis
plans before data are seen. A Claim Card records the assumptions behind a
single verdict. Like a preregistration, it exists before any evidence is
gathered, and it is saved with the report.

blocks.en:
Some disagreements between a run and a gold label may be disagreements
about what the claim means (Section 6 ), and the
experts’ own calculations show one way this can arise. The experts
assessed two claims through proxies computed with CHGNet. For
the Fe-doped Co 3 O 4 claim, the expert used the total magnetic moment
as a proxy for saturation magnetization, whereas the frozen card named
saturation magnetization itself. The expert’s proxy for stiffness on the
Mg-in-Al stiffening claim was the bulk modulus, and the frozen card named
Young’s modulus. On these
claims a run and the expert may have assessed different observables, so a
run that disagrees with the gold label has not necessarily reached a wrong
verdict.

Runs with the computational tools that obtained the same calculation still

reaction meant two coexisting phases or AlCu coexisting with a
lithium-containing phase (Appendices F and F.1 ). Since the two groups of runs come from different
conditions, the contrast may also reflect their other differences. Part of
the decision can be made by the coding agent, because each playbook asks
it for its own score under tolerances that no card field sets
(Appendix J ). We think the computational tools move
part of the ambiguity from what evidence the agent can find to how it
judges a computed value against the claim.

blocks.en:
Some of what decided the verdicts is not on the card. On the Fe–Al
Al 2 Fe-onset claim, all five frozen runs computed the same B2 limit
under one card whose quantifier was typical, and their scores still ranged
from + 2 +2 to − 1 -1 . Two of them had committed in their first reasoning step
to scoring it negative on a single matched counterexample. The card holds the
quantifier from which that rule follows, but not which result counts as a
counterexample. In one card run on the Al–Mg–Zn τ \tau -phase claim, the
report and the card disagreed on the quantifier
(Appendix G ).
A decision-rule field could state, before any evidence is gathered, what
result would refute the claim, and a tolerance field could give the coding
agent the card’s threshold in place of the playbook’s defaults. We would
test these two fields. Other choices that can decide a computational
verdict could also become fields, among them an equilibrium or a kinetic
(Scheil) treatment of solidification, the composition basis (atomic or
weight percent), the basis of a phase fraction (mole or volume), the
thermodynamic database and the numerical tolerances.

Card runs receive the

system, route or deployment claims, with material viability, integration
budgets closed with margin, controls and operations, and manufacturability
as its elements. The rest differs only in typography. The section’s “lock before tools” means that the agent records the
card before it uses a tool. It does not refer to the frozen condition.
The guideline tells the agent elsewhere to “prefer the weakest faithful
interpretation of a claim.”

AND / OR semantics ; disjunctive parts interpreted as ** OR ** unless stated otherwise ). - ** Sufficiency set ** for * system / method / deployment * claims : the minimal elements that must simultaneously hold ( method validity , boundary conditions closed with margin , controls , reproducibility ). - ** Assumed defaults ** when the text is silent ( see 1.6), and ** near - match tolerances ** you will accept later ( see 4.2). - ** What would decisively change the score ** ( pre - register the minimal decisive evidence ). - ** Provenance **: for each entry above , mark whether it is * stated * in the claim text , * inferred * from the text with domain knowledge , or a * default * you assumed because the text is silent .

blocks.en: ⬇ A system wrote a structured interpretation ( a " Claim Card ") of a scientific claim before assessing it . Audit the card against the claim . blocks.en: ⬇ A system wrote a structured interpretation ( a " Claim Card ") of a scientific claim . Independently , a domain expert judged the claim and wrote a rationale . Claim : { claim } Claim Card : { card } Expert rationale : { rationale } Does the expert rationale rely on a reading of the claim that the Claim Card excludes ? Answer " compatible " if the expert ’ s reading fits within the card , " excluded " if the expert reads the claim in a way the card rules out ( for example a different system , scope , quantifier , threshold , or comparator ), or " unclear " if the rationale does not show how the expert read the claim .
